n: Moroni explains how people qualified for baptism, including those who would serve as elders, priests, and teachers. Each had to show by their lives that they were ready, not just say so.

f.g: fruit suitable or fitting; evidence in one’s life that matches true repentance.

n: Baptism required real humility — a broken heart and contrite spirit — and an honest witness to the church that one had repented of all sins. It was a serious covenant, not a casual ceremony.

f.w: a broken heart and a contrite spirit

f.g: deeply sorry for sin; humbled and teachable.

n: Candidates also took Christ’s name upon themselves and determined to serve him for the rest of their lives. Baptism marks a beginning, not a finish line.

f.w: took upon them the name of Christ

n: After baptism and the cleansing power of the Holy Ghost, new members were recorded by name so the church could remember and nourish them. Fellowship, scripture, and prayer kept them on the path, trusting entirely in Christ’s merits.

f.w: relying alone upon the merits of Christ
the author and the finisher of their faith

n: The church met frequently to fast, pray, and talk with one another about their spiritual well-being. Church was a community that cared for each soul.
They also met often to partake of the sacrament in remembrance of Jesus — the same pattern Latter-day Saints follow in weekly sacrament meeting.
The church guarded its members’ integrity. Serious sin was judged with the testimony of witnesses before the elders, and those who would not repent were removed from membership.
Yet the door always stayed open. Whenever people sincerely repented and asked forgiveness, they were forgiven — a powerful reassurance of the Lord’s patience.

f.g: genuine purpose; meaning it with the whole heart.

n: Meetings were led by the Spirit: whether someone preached, exhorted, prayed, or sang depended on how the Holy Ghost guided them. The same principle is taught for latter-day meetings.

f.w: conducted by the church after the manner of the workings of the Spirit
